stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist takes an oral controlled-substance prescription from a caller she has never dealt with, reduces it to writing at once, and dispenses. Eight days later no electronic prescription has arrived and the prescriber holds no commissioner exception from electronic prescribing. What has gone wrong?

choices.text: Nothing; the pharmacist's written record is the complete requirement.
Only that the pharmacist should have refused an oral prescription outright.
Only that the written record should have been made within two days rather than at once.
The pharmacist should have obtained the prescription in writing before dispensing.
No reasonable effort was made to verify the caller, and the two-day follow-up has lapsed.

explanation.core_reasoning: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(b) requires the pharmacist, where the prescribing practitioner is NOT KNOWN to her, to make a REASONABLE EFFORT to determine that the oral authorization came from a registered practitioner. Section 20(c) requires the practitioner to cause an ELECTRONIC prescription to reach the dispensing pharmacy WITHIN 2 DAYS, the seven-day written route being available only where the commissioner has granted an exception. Both limbs have failed here.

choice_analysis.A: The written record answers s. 20(a) only.
choice_analysis.B: Oral prescriptions are permitted in the circumstances the statute allows.
choice_analysis.C: Reducing to writing immediately is what s. 20(a) requires.
choice_analysis.D: That would defeat the oral prescription route entirely.
choice_analysis.E: Correct on both the verification duty and the follow-up window.

related_facts: The pharmacy attaches the follow-up prescription to the record it reduced to writing
explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates treat the written record as the whole of the oral prescription procedure.

reasoning_steps: Note that the caller was unknown to the pharmacist
Apply the two-day electronic follow-up, the seven-day route needing an exception
